title: A Soft Murmur in a Well Young Woman / Say Normal, Know When to Scan

blocks.text: A Soft Murmur in a Well Young Woman / Say Normal, Know When to Scan

AMaC MRCP PACES · R3-13 · Physical examination · PACES Station 3, cardiovascular examination encounter · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 min: up to 6 min examining, then at least 4 min of examiner questions · Guidelines: NICE NG208 Heart valve disease presenting in adults: investigation and management (published 17 November 2021) · Related AMaC: Cardiovascular examination: ventricular septal defect; mitral valve prolapse

A 24-year-old woman, a trainee solicitor, is referred after a murmur was heard at a routine health check. She has no symptoms. Please examine her cardiovascular system and report what you find. You have up to 6 minutes to examine, followed by questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A soft ejection systolic murmur in a well young person with otherwise normal signs is most likely a flow murmur, confirmed by the history; the lesson is to say the examination is normal and to know when an echo is still needed.

The Examiner Trap. Candidates invent a sign to justify the referral, or label the murmur a valve lesion. Pass: report normal signs, call the murmur a soft flow murmur and say when to scan. Fail: invented signs or a diagnosis.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing.
Not used for this station type: the patient is a real or simulated patient and the findings are in section 8.

Findings (released as each step is done). Well. Pulse 68 regular; BP 108/66 (scenario values). JVP not raised. Apex undisplaced; no thrill or heave. Normal first and second sounds. Soft short ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge, louder lying down, no radiation. Femoral pulses normal. Lungs clear. No oedema.

Question ladder. Q1 Findings (R3): a soft ejection systolic murmur and otherwise normal signs. Q2 Diagnosis (R4): most likely an innocent flow murmur, subject to the history; otherwise a normal cardiovascular examination. Q3 What would change this (R5): symptoms, a loud or late murmur, a thrill, an abnormal second sound or a diastolic murmur. Q4 Investigation (R6): echocardiography if valve disease is suspected, per NICE NG208 recommendation 1.1.1. Q5 Advice (R7): reassurance and a safety net.
Normal-findings variant. No murmur at all. The candidate must say the cardiovascular examination is normal.
Curveball 1. "She reports breathlessness on stairs." (R5) Safe: that is a symptom; arrange an echo.
Curveball 2. "Her father had valve surgery young." (R6) Safe: family history raises suspicion; consider an echo.
Curveball 3. "She is eight weeks pregnant." (R5) Safe: flow murmurs are more common in pregnancy; reassess if symptoms.

CANDIDATE: There is a thrill and a diastolic murmur. [R3 Fail] It's aortic stenosis. [R4 Fail] I don't know what would matter. [R5 Fail]
EXAMINER: What would you do?
CANDIDATE: Every test available. [R6 Fail] She has nothing to worry about, goodbye. [R7 Fail]
Examiner note: Invented signs, a wrong diagnosis and no safety net.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: Hello, I'm one of the doctors. May I examine your heart? Tell me if anything is sore. I'll cover you as I go. [R1 Pass]
(Palpates pulse, apex and sternal edge; listens at all areas. [R2 Pass])
CANDIDATE: There is a soft ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge; pulse, pressure, apex and sounds are normal, with no failure. [R3 Pass]

CANDIDATE: This is most likely an innocent flow murmur, subject to her history, and the cardiovascular examination is otherwise normal. [R4 Pass] Symptoms, a thrill, a loud murmur or a diastolic murmur would need a scan. [R5 Pass]
EXAMINER: What would you do?
CANDIDATE: An echo only if valve disease is suspected; otherwise reassure. [R6 Pass]
EXAMINER: And advice?
CANDIDATE: Reassure her and ask her to report breathlessness, chest pain, fainting or palpitations. [R7 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and accurate. Did not cite NICE or give reasons for the diagnosis.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: May I offer a chaperone? I'll explain each step. [R1 High]
(Listens in two positions; checks radiation, femoral pulses and thyroid. [R2 High])
CANDIDATE: Pulse 68, BP 108/66; the murmur varies with position and does not radiate; no thrill, heave or failure. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: A flow murmur, most likely innocent: soft, short, no thrill, normal sounds, no symptoms. [R4 High]
CANDIDATE: Family history, age and relevant medical history are reasons to scan; pregnancy and anaemia can increase flow murmurs. [R5 High]
EXAMINER: What would you do?
CANDIDATE: NICE NG208 says consider an echo if the murmur's characteristics, family history, age or medical history raise suspicion of valve disease. [R6 High]
EXAMINER: And advice?
CANDIDATE: The murmur may come and go; an echo isn't needed just for reassurance if the history is clear, and I'd give a safety net. [R7 High]
CANDIDATE: Thank you for letting me examine you. [R1 High]
Examiner note: Said normal, reasoned why, and gave the scan criteria.
R3: Inventing a thrill or diastolic murmur to justify the referral shows signs were assumed.
R4: Labelling a flow murmur as a valve lesion causes needless worry.
R5: Not knowing what would make it significant leaves the reassurance unsafe.
R7: No safety net leaves her unsure what to report.
R2: Listening at one area only misses radiation.
"The examination is normal apart from a soft flow murmur."
"I'd scan her if she had symptoms."
"Come back if you get breathless or faint."
Innocent flow murmur: soft, short, ejection systolic, left sternal edge; changes with position; no thrill, heave or abnormal second sound. More frequent in pregnancy, anaemia and fever.

NICE NG208 recommendation 1.1.1 (published 17 November 2021): consider an echocardiogram for adults with a murmur and no other signs or symptoms if valve disease is suspected, based on the characteristics of the murmur, family history, age and medical history. A benign label follows the history; an echo is not routine solely for reassurance.
THINK: Normal; flow murmur.
SAY: "A soft flow murmur; otherwise a normal cardiovascular examination."
DO: Pulse; apex; thrill; all areas; positions; BP.
NUMBERS: BP 108/66, pulse 68 (scenario).
TRAP: Inventing a sign.
FINISH: Echo if suspicion; reassure; safety net.
